手持樂器，以敲擊方式發聲。手持樂器本體，透過敲擊、搖晃、刮奏或撥彈等方式使樂器本: A hand-held instrument, sounding by being struck. The player holds the instrument itself and makes it vibrate by striking, shaking, scraping or plucking it. Different parts and different amounts of force give different timbres. When practising, first check that the instrument is held correctly, and once the basic way of sounding it is secure, work on rhythm patterns and melodies. The instrument is held in one hand and shaken from the wrist, so that the grains inside or the parts on the outside strike it and make it sound.
津巴布韋傳統體鳴樂器霍紹鼓，Hornbostel–Sachs編號112.13，由: The hosho is a traditional idiophone of Zimbabwe, Hornbostel–Sachs 112.13, made from a pair of maranka (mapudzi) gourds filled with hota (canna) seeds. Once the gourds have been boiled in salt water and their insides scraped out, the timbre is sharper and the attack stronger. It rattles when played and is common in Shona music, in mbira ensembles and on occasions such as mhande, and it is also a route by which women take part in mbira playing.

荷索鼓源於非洲南部的津巴布韋，是肖納人傳統音樂文化的重要組成部分。這種樂器由一對: The hosho comes from Zimbabwe in southern Africa and is an important part of traditional Shona musical culture. The instrument consists of a pair of gourds filled with hota seeds, shaken to produce a crisp percussive sound. Its traditional making is a fine craft: the maker first boils the gourds in salt water and then carefully clears out the inside to get the best sound. The hosho plays a key role in the development of Shona music, above all as the main accompanying instrument in mbira bands and in traditional ceremonial music. As African traditional music has been promoted internationally, the hosho's influence has spread beyond Zimbabwe's borders. In the contemporary world music movement its distinctive timbre and cultural meaning have drawn the attention of ethnomusicologists and musicians around the world, and it has become an important medium of exchange in African traditional music.
荷索鼓音色明亮清脆，具有乾爽的打擊感，帶著獨特的沙沙律動。其音域位於中高頻，聲音: The hosho's timbre is bright and crisp, with a dry attack and a distinctive rustling motion. It lies in the upper middle frequencies and penetrates well, cutting clearly through the lines of other instruments. Because the gourds are filled with canna seeds, it resonates by the seeds striking the gourd, giving a grainy sound with many layers. Compared with the mbira the hosho is lighter and more flexible; compared with African drums its sound is finer and more rhythmic. After the inside has been cleaned out the timbre is sharper and more forceful, which raises its power as an accompanying instrument, and in traditional Shona music it keeps the rhythm steady and supports the melody.
霍紹鼓 主要出現在辛巴威紹納音樂的合奏場合，尤其常見於 mbira（姆比拉）合奏: The hosho appears mainly in ensemble settings of Shona music in Zimbabwe, and is especially common in mbira ensembles and in traditional types such as mhande. It is also used to accompany Shona music and forms an important rhythmic layer in marimba music. Makwa clapping and whistling often appear with the hosho, and are found in ngoma and in mbira ensembles. The machachara (miniature hosho made from shells or bottle caps) are also often attached to the mbira as an extra rattle. In the eyes of mbira players the hosho often leads rather than merely accompanies; Oliver Mtukudzi also holds that it keeps the musicians in step, and Tendai Kazuru is named as a respected hosho player.
霍紹鼓 為辛巴威體鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 112.13。: The hosho is a Zimbabwean idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 112.13. The common form has a pair of maranka (mapudzi) gourds as its body, with hota (canna) seeds inside to sound; in making it the gourds are first boiled in salt water and the residue inside is then scraped out with a corncob, a plug of newspaper or woven metal wire. Smaller versions are made from the wild orange damba, bound together with sticks and filled with hota seeds or pebbles. The source also mentions the machachara, a small hosho made of shells or bottle caps. The materials of the other parts are not stated.
